newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil millers want option of U.S. wheat imports.
newsitem.headline: Brazil millers want option of U.S. wheat imports.

text.p: Brazilian millers are experiencing problems obtaining quality wheat and are hoping discussions with U.S. government officials will resolve current problems over phytosanitary requirements, millers said.
"We need quality wheat and we are hoping the Brazilian government will be sensitive to this," one miller said.

Brazilian and U.S. officials have been negotiating over stricter Brazilian entry requirements for wheat which in theory took effect as of January 1 last year but which only came into practice after a waiver expired at the end of September.
The current problems center on the tilletia controversa kuhn (TCK) fungus which has been found only in very limited areas in northern U.S. states, government officials said.
But because U.S. inspectors do not normally know the origin of the wheat, they are unable to guarantee "free of TCK" on a federal certificate as is necessary under the new rules.
The U.S. was not expected to export much, if any, wheat to Brazil this year given a bumper 1996/97 Argentine harvest.
But with some Argentine wheat not of the quality millers need, purchases from Brazil's Mercosur partner Argentina so far are estimated at most three million tonnes.
Last month there were rumors a visiting Canadian delegation had sold 600,000 tonnes to Brazil but weeks later, millers say only around 300,000 tonnes were agreed.
This would bring total purchases so far of Canadian wheat to around 500,000 tonnes and ideally Brazil would like to buy a further 500,000 tonnes, they said.
But Brazil is still likely to need another million tonnes which ideally would involve 500,000 tonnes from the U.S.
For the time being, millers have enough wheat to last one more month, traders said.

But despite the fact cargoes would therefore need to be booked soon, few are willing to gamble on the two governments resolving the TCK problem, especially after one company's disastrous attempt last year to bring in two ships carrying German wheat, believed to be infected with TCK.
"Nobody wants to take the risk as we don't need the bad publicity and we are worried that it would be just the same as the German case last year," one miller said.

Government officials are hoping Brazil's Agriculture Minister Arlindo Porto will take advantage of a current trip to Washington to meet U.S. Agriculture Department Secretary Dan Glickman and discuss the issue.
